explanations.answer: God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, "Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." (2 Thessalonians 1:2) Notice where the gift comes from. It isn't from Paul or his team. It comes from the Father and the Son.

explanations.answer: Paul and the churches of Judea
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but Paul isn't handing out grace from his own pocket. He says it comes "…from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." (2 Thessalonians 1:2) Judea never shows up in this greeting. Paul is just the one passing the note along.

explanations.answer: The apostles and elders in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Jerusalem sounds official, I'll give you that. But Paul's greeting never mentions the apostles or elders. He says the grace and peace come "…from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." (2 Thessalonians 1:2) The source is God Himself, not a committee.
Growing, baker! Paul says their "…faith is growing more and more…" (2 Thessalonians 1:3) Not a little. More and more. That's the kind of rising I wish my dough would do on a cold morning.

Fading is the opposite of what Paul says. He writes that their "…faith is growing more and more…" (2 Thessalonians 1:3) Nothing in his thanks sounds like a flame getting low. This is a church on the way up.

Wavering sounds like a wobbly cookie cutter near the edge of the counter, and I've caught a few of those. But Paul says the Thessalonians' faith is "…growing more and more…" (2 Thessalonians 1:3) That's the word he picked, and it's the opposite of fading. Wavering isn't what he thanks God for here.
Not quite, friend. Paul says the opposite: their "…love for one another is increasing." (2 Thessalonians 1:3) Nothing is cooling off here. Their love is going up, right along with their faith.
False is right, baker. Paul says their "…love for one another is increasing." (2 Thessalonians 1:3) So this love isn't cooling off, it's heating up. Better than any oven in my bakery.

That's it, baker. Paul says he boasts "…about your perseverance and faith in the face of all the persecution and affliction you are enduring." (2 Thessalonians 1:4) He's bragging on how they keep going. I'd be the same way about my six cookie cutter kids.

Giving is a good thing, but it's not what Paul brags about here. He boasts about their "…perseverance and faith…" (2 Thessalonians 1:4) The letter doesn't mention their giving in this passage. It's all about how they hold on.

Teachers are a blessing, friend, but they don't come up in this boast. Paul says he boasts about the Thessalonians' "…perseverance and faith…" (2 Thessalonians 1:4) He's proud of the church members themselves, and how they keep standing.

Right, baker. Paul says they keep going "…in the face of all the persecution and affliction you are enduring." (2 Thessalonians 1:4) That word "all" matters. This church wasn't having an easy time. I think that makes their perseverance even sweeter.

explanations.answer: A long famine in the land
explanations.explanation: No famine in this letter, friend. Paul says they hold on "…in the face of all the persecution and affliction you are enduring." (2 Thessalonians 1:4) The trouble he names is persecution and affliction, not an empty pantry.

Good guess, since churches have their moments, but Paul says something different. He praises their love for one another (2 Thessalonians 1:3). The trouble he names is "…persecution and affliction…" (2 Thessalonians 1:4) That's what they're enduring, and quarrels aren't in the verse.

Careful, friend. Paul says the opposite. He writes, "…you will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering." (2 Thessalonians 1:5) Their suffering isn't a sign they're out. Paul says they will be counted worthy.

False is right, baker. Paul says, "…you will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering." (2 Thessalonians 1:5) So the suffering doesn't say "not worthy." He tells them they will be counted worthy of the kingdom.

Relief it is, baker. Paul says it's right "…to grant relief to you who are oppressed…" (2 Thessalonians 1:7) After all that affliction, relief is the word. I think any tired baker knows how good that sounds.
Riches would be a nice surprise, but that's not on Paul's list. He says God will "…grant relief to you who are oppressed…" (2 Thessalonians 1:7) What he promises is relief.

Honor is a good word, friend, but it's not what Paul names here. He says God will "…grant relief to you who are oppressed…" (2 Thessalonians 1:7) For people under pressure, relief is the gift in view.

Close, but no, friend. Paul says God will "…grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well." (2 Thessalonians 1:7) Did you catch "…and to us as well."? Paul and his team are in on the relief too.

False is right, baker. Paul says God will "…grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well." (2 Thessalonians 1:7) He puts himself and his team in that line right next to the oppressed Thessalonians. The relief isn't for them only.
Heaven, baker! Paul says this happens "…when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels" (2 Thessalonians 1:7) He isn't coming from a city or a building. He's revealed from heaven.

Jerusalem is a big name in the Bible, friend, but it's not the answer here. Paul says the Lord Jesus is "…revealed from heaven with His mighty angels" (2 Thessalonians 1:7) The reveal comes from heaven itself.
The temple was a famous place, but Paul doesn't point there. He says the Lord Jesus is "…revealed from heaven with His mighty angels" (2 Thessalonians 1:7) The answer is heaven.

explanations.answer: Those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Paul says Jesus is "…inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus." (2 Thessalonians 1:8) This is a heavy part, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously. The text names who it's for, so we keep to what it says.

explanations.answer: Those who never kept the feasts in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The feasts aren't mentioned here, friend. Paul says the vengeance is on "…those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus." (2 Thessalonians 1:8) This is a heavy verse, so it's good to read it exactly as written.

explanations.answer: Those who never made an offering at the temple
explanations.explanation: Offerings aren't the point in this verse. Paul says the vengeance is on "…those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus." (2 Thessalonians 1:8) I think this is one of the heavier lines in the letter, so it helps to stay with the exact words.

True, baker. Paul says Jesus comes "…to be glorified in His saints and regarded with wonder by all who have believed, including you who have believed our testimony." (2 Thessalonians 1:10) See that "including you"? The Thessalonians are right there in the crowd.

Not this time, friend. Paul says Jesus will be "…regarded with wonder by all who have believed, including you who have believed our testimony." (2 Thessalonians 1:10) The Thessalonians are named right in the verse. They're included.
His calling, baker! Paul prays "…that our God will count you worthy of His calling…" (2 Thessalonians 1:11) The calling belongs to God, and Paul is asking God to count them worthy of it.

A place of honor sounds like a front-row seat, friend, and I'd take one at the cookie table. But Paul doesn't pray for that. He prays that God "…will count you worthy of His calling…" (2 Thessalonians 1:11) The prize in his prayer is God's calling, not a seat.

A peaceful life would sure be a gift, and I'd take a quiet morning with a warm oven myself. But Paul doesn't pray for that here. He prays that God "…will count you worthy of His calling…" (2 Thessalonians 1:11) Remember, these folks are enduring persecution and affliction (2 Thessalonians 1:4), and his prayer points to the calling.

explanations.answer: Fulfill every good desire and work of faith
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul prays that God "…will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith…" (2 Thessalonians 1:11) Every good desire, every work of faith. I like how big that prayer is.

explanations.answer: Turn every one of their enemies into friends
explanations.explanation: That would be a plot twist, but Paul doesn't pray it. He asks that God "…will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith…" (2 Thessalonians 1:11) Nothing here about changing their enemies.

explanations.answer: Make them leaders over every nearby city
explanations.explanation: Leaders over cities is a big job, friend, and Paul never asks for it. He prays that God "…will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith…" (2 Thessalonians 1:11) The prayer is about their good desires and their work of faith.

Glorified, baker! Paul says "…so that the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you, and you in Him…" (2 Thessalonians 1:12) Jesus' name is glorified in them, and they are in Him. And the whole point is His name.

Proclaimed is a strong word, friend, and it sounds like something a preacher would say. But Paul writes that "…the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you, and you in Him…" (2 Thessalonians 1:12) His prayer is that Jesus' name is glorified, not just announced.

Remembered is a sweet word, and I know a thing or two about wanting to be remembered. But Paul says "…the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you, and you in Him…" (2 Thessalonians 1:12) Glorified is the answer.
